items.title: Jang interviewed by Monk Rowe, 2013
items.q: So you play the same music all the time. You know, Monk, you commented about how you had to play in a rock group... So to kind of deal with the boredom at times you improvise before the production or the concert started.

ctx.x: How does something like that come about? You have this, your own passion for history, American history and the role of Chinese people in it, and you want to compose music that addresses it, but what’s the process of getting a symphony written and than having people play it?

Oh it’s been a lifelong process. And that’s actually somewhat of a separate question, but then what I would describe that this has been an idea that germinated since my childhood. During the 1960’s I spent my childhood in Palo Alto, and that’s located, that’s where Stanford University is located. And I was often reminded that Stanford built the railroad. © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -1-

So in 1963 the Chinese Historical Society of America was founded, and my uncle Philip Choy was one of the longtime leaders. He wasn’t a founder, but he was a longtime leader. And in 1969, which was supposed to be the celebration of the centennial anniversary of the completion of the transcontinental railroad, which was held in Utah and was celebrated by the U.S. government, there was a keynote speaker named John Volpe, he was the secretary of transportation.
